Even standard metrics such as production cost savings are subject to disagreements over input assumptions and model scenarios used to quantify the benefits. In addition, the estimated benefits quantified ex ante through various models can vary across different future scenarios and be very different from realized benefits ex post in operations (Shu and Mays 2025). Further, the nature and magnitude of benefits may change over the lifetime of the project. One recommended approach to address these challenges is to allocate costs “roughly commensurate” with, but not formulaically based on, quantified benefits (Pfeifenberger, 2025). Network usage is generally accepted as a proxy for how much each network user benefits from a transmission facility. Here, too, there are implementation challenges because there is no universally accepted method to measure how much each agent uses the network (Olmos 2006). In 2024, FERC passed Order 1920, which focuses on long-term regional transmission planning and cost allocation (FERC 2024a). Similar to Order 1000, the regulations for cost allocation reinforced the principle of “beneficiary pays.” These were focused on high-level principles2 and process improvements for developing cost allocation methods rather than methods themselves, and these regulations leave transmission providers with the flexibility to design their own approach for transmission cost allocation.
